name: ransom_note_scan
description: Find files whose names look like ransom notes (a name match is a CANDIDATE, not a note) and locate what is in them without printing it. Each candidate is read once (up to max_size, 16 MiB at most), decoded by byte-order mark, then by the NUL pattern of UTF-16 without one, else UTF-8 (decoding errors counted; a binary file is listed and not read as text), and classified `content_resembles_note` when its content shows at least two kinds of note marker (an onion address, a wallet, a Tox id, a labelled identifier, note vocabulary) and otherwise `filename_only`; neither confirms a note. Indicator candidates are found by pattern: onion addresses, e-mail addresses, URLs, bitcoin, monero and ethereum addresses, Tox ids and the value after a label such as "your personal ID" (kind identifier_candidate); a bitcoin address's own checksum is checked (checksum_valid, checksum_failed) and the rest are syntactic candidates, none attributed to anyone. The answer is a locator: per note its id, size, sha256 of the whole file (withheld, with the reason, for a note shorter than 128 bytes or one that is a single token or indicator value, where it would be a digest of the value), modification time (raw nanoseconds and ISO UTC, as collected), class, encoding, decoding errors and a count per kind; per occurrence its finding id, byte offset, length and validation. No identifier, wallet, address, URL, key or note text is in the answer or in any file it names, and any path component that holds an identifier-shaped token (a run of 8 or more letters and digits holding both, a run of 10 or more digits, or a run of 8 or more letters that is not one word, a capitalised word, several capitalised words or all capitals), a token, key or user-info the shared withholding rules find, or a value the note held, is withheld from every path it prints (notes, rejected name matches, directories it could not list, exclusions, the root) and counted once per printed path in paths_withheld. The identifier shape is a guess and its rates were measured on 5,000 random draws per shape as a directory name (unicode folded first): a token that is groups of four joined by a dash, an underscore or a dot, and any token of seven characters or fewer, is printed (100%); a random 8-character letters-and-digits token is printed 3.3% of the time (9 characters 2.2%, 12 characters 0.6%, 16 characters 0.1%), base32 of 16 characters 3.6%, 8 lower-case letters and digits 7.1%, 12 full-width letters and digits 0.7%, 24 letters 0.03%, and none of hex of 16, 32 or 64 characters, 12 or 20 decimal digits, a UUID or base58 of 22 characters. On a developer machine's application, cache and package trees the same rule withheld 4.9% of 600,000 real directory components (dates, versions and package ids hold digits among letters) and some component of 38% of their directories, so a harmless name is often withheld: list the directory for it. Names are judged by shape only: an identifier of another shape is printed. SENSITIVE: a note can hold access tokens. write_values: true (refused outside a job, and in a job whose process lacks SECRET_OUTPUT=1; the manifest makes every job that sets write_values secret output) creates $OUT/ransom-note-values.jsonl, mode 0600, before it scans (a file or link already there is refused by name) and writes the values, a preview of each note's first lines and the real paths to it and nowhere else. It follows no link and reads only regular files; every name match it did not read (a link, a special file, empty, over max_size, unreadable) is listed with the reason, and `status` (also `complete`) says `partial`, with `status_basis`, when one could have held something or the time limit (max_seconds, default 480, below the manifest's 600) stopped the walk, naming how many entries and directories were not examined. A stop signal (SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGHUP) ends it with one JSON answer (status failed, interrupted, exit code 128 + the signal) after removing the pages it was writing; a values file already begun is kept, cut back to its last whole row, and the answer says how many rows it holds. A page file already there is never replaced: the new one takes the next free name, and the answer names it. The earliest note time is an observation of the filesystem's mtime as collected, not the start of the run. A note named otherwise, an image of a note, an encoding it does not detect and a long unlabelled token (no label, no known shape: a 64-digit hex string after the word "Token") are not found, not located and not counted. Takes a directory tree, so it has no `use` triggers.

root.description: A directory to sweep (an extracted tree, not an image)

max_size.description: Largest file to read as a note (default 200000, at least 16, at most 16777216); a name match above it is listed as not read, with its size

limit.description: Rows shown inline per table (default 100); every row is counted, and a table with more is written whole as JSON Lines and named in pages.<table>.all_results

write_values.description: Write each value found, and a preview of each note, to $OUT/ransom-note-values.jsonl (default false). Refused unless the tool runs as a job run as secret output (the manifest makes a job that sets this one; the tool checks SECRET_OUTPUT=1 in its environment); the file is created first and a file or link already there is refused; the answer never carries a value

exclude_top_level_dirs.description: Directory names skipped at the top of the root only (default ["proc", "sys", "dev"]); each is listed as an exclusion. [] excludes nothing; a directory of that name deeper in the tree is always read

max_seconds.description: The tool's own time limit in seconds (default 480, at most 540; the manifest's timeout is 600). When it runs out the walk stops, what was read is written, and the answer is partial and says how many entries and directories were not examined. A note being scanned when it runs out is finished first
